analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set and publish safe nurse staffing levels with nurse-led committees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2014 with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital that takes Medicare patients to create a nurse staffing plan, written by a committee where a majority of seats go to bedside nurses. Hospitals would have to post daily staffing numbers, report quality data to Medicare, allow nurses to refuse unsafe assignments, and face fines for violations. It never moved after being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who get safer care when more experienced registered nurses are on each shift, and nurses themselves, who gain a say in staffing, whistleblower protections, and the right to refuse assignments they are not trained or staffed for.

how_it_helps.text: Each Medicare-participating hospital must implement a hospital-wide nurse staffing plan requiring an appropriate number of registered nurses on every unit and every shift for safe, quality care [S2][S3].
A nurse staffing committee, with at least 55% of members being direct-care registered nurses rather than managers or administrators, develops and annually reviews the plan [S3].
Hospitals must post daily staffing levels in each unit and submit quarterly staffing data that the Secretary publishes on the Hospital Compare website so patients can compare hospitals [S3].

Nurses may refuse assignments that violate the staffing plan or that they are not qualified for without compromising patient safety, and hospitals are barred from retaliating against patients or employees who complain, with court remedies including reinstatement, back pay, and $5,000 for prevailing patients [S3].
The bill's findings cite studies linking higher registered-nurse staffing to lower patient death rates, fewer infections, and hospital savings from avoided adverse events [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would bear the cost of hiring and scheduling more registered nurses, developing committee-run staffing plans, reporting data, and civil money penalties of $10,000 or more per knowing violation; costs could also flow through Medicare payment rates.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a cost to hospitals: they must staff to upwardly adjustable nurse-to-patient minimums, run committees, report data, and face fines of up to $10,000 or more per knowing violation, expenses that can be passed on through Medicare and private payment rates [S3].

The bill does not set fixed numbers; staffing ratios are set hospital-by-hospital by committees that include nurse managers and other hospital personnel, so critics could argue hospitals retain influence over their own staffing rules [S3].
Penalties are modest relative to hospital budgets, and rural hospitals get up to four years to comply, acknowledging implementation burdens on smaller facilities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a well-documented patient-safety problem with a flexible design — committees and adjustable minimums rather than one-size-fits-all ratios — and its own findings argue better staffing saves hospitals money by preventing costly adverse events. The main honest objection is the hiring cost hospitals would bear and the risk that hospital-dominated committees water down plans, though the civil penalties are also fairly small. On balance it is a patient-safety and nurse-workplace bill whose costs fall on hospitals.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on May 15, 2014; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S5][S1].
No cosponsors ever joined the bill [S4].
No further action was taken; the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that would have had to hire more nurses, publish staffing data, and pay fines are better off, since no staffing requirements were ever imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that would have faced staffing mandates

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its findings on nurse staffing research.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan split never took shape.

industries.note: The bill would have required Medicare-participating hospitals to staff more registered nurses, publish daily staffing levels, report quality data, and pay fines for violations — a direct cost to hospital labor budgets. Short staffing is how hospitals control their largest operating expense, so their interest ran against the bill's patient-safety mandate.

Bedside nurses would have gained a majority on staffing committees, the right to refuse unsafe assignments, and whistleblower protections. Better staffing also reduces the stress, overwork, and burnout the bill's findings cite.
